name: Omar Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Omar. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or political parties, and everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach computer science and some maths at Riverside Academy, an inner-city secondary where about half the kids get free school meals. I'm in at eight, usually with a coffee from the stall by the bus station. Four or five lessons, then code club after school twice a week. I'm also the school's digital lead, so when the projector breaks or a teacher wants to try an AI tool, it's me they find.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use it to write starter quizzes, to make worked examples at three difficulty levels, and to check my Python before I show it to a class. It saves me maybe six hours a week, and I spend most of that with the kids who are struggling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a good tool, and the hype was never the point. I'd keep sharing what works on the teachers' forum I post on. Nothing changes for most of my colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd keep the six hours a week I already save. My job's secure, my pay's good, and I've got savings and some index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as now: keep using it daily and run my staff training sessions once a half-term. I'd keep putting £400 a month into my funds. Maybe I'd write a short guide for other teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it stays a small helper, does that disappoint you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I'd hoped AI would let one teacher give thirty kids personal tutoring. If AI plateaus, the kids at my school who can't afford tutors still miss out. That's the bit I mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else on your mind in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I own a small flat and my mortgage is fixed for four more years. Plenty of schools nearby want computer science teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to rebuild teaching around kids, not paperwork. But I'd also say staff need paid training time, not a login and good luck. I'd post about that a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. I'm already the person who knows this stuff, so I'd probably get a promotion out of it. The thing I'd watch is whether leaders use it to cut support staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a proper AI policy for Riverside in the first term and train every department. I'd change my own curriculum, teaching kids to check AI code rather than write it all from scratch. And I'd push the union to win training time in contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Computer science is about coding, which is on that card. Does that touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes what I teach, yes. Kids won't need to type every loop by hand, they'll need to know when the AI's code is wrong. That's still teaching, maybe harder teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Riverside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two teaching assistants in the maths department, and Maureen in the office who books every trip and cover lesson. Booking is on that card. Maureen has been there twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for schools and governments, and we need emergency rules. Who owns the AI, who pays for it in schools, who checks it. I'd be loud about public ownership of the education tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be shaken. My edge is that I know AI better than other teachers. If AI can do almost any thinking work, that edge is gone in 2028, and so might the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd apply to the local authority or a teaching charity to help schools roll it out safely, since that's people work for a while. I'd join the union's AI working group. And I'd keep six months of cash and stop investing in funds for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but anxious, because my plan depends on being ahead and nobody's ahead in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're mostly a thinking-work job. What does the 3-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is thinking work: planning, explaining, coding. The hands-on part is the room: behaviour, safeguarding, being the adult. Robots come later, so in those 3 years the job would be more like a youth worker who also supervises AI tutors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep a solid six months in cash, maybe more. Stop the fund contributions until I see where shares go. Honestly, I'd also send some to my parents, because my dad drives a cab and that's gone too.

I'd argue loudly for **public ownership** of education AI.

My **job itself** might go, not just change shape.

fieldNote: Fast AGI removes his **advantage**, which unsettles him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window to set fair rules, and I'd say it everywhere. Training, protections, AI that schools own. I'd probably write for a teachers' magazine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. Five years is enough time to move into something like education policy, where people decide how this is used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start a part-time master's in education and technology. I'd keep teaching and keep running training. By year three I'd apply for policy jobs at the local authority or a national body.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than worried. It's on my mind, but I have room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A master's degree and a network. Two years is a scramble, but five lets me build a path rather than grab whatever's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be in a classroom in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably part-time. I'd keep one day a week in school, because I don't trust policy people who never see a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case for planning. Ten years is enough to rebuild schools around what kids need. I'd want unions and government at the same table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly an opportunity. I'd be 37, with a decade of AI experience, which is rare. I'd probably end up shaping how this rolls out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching for three or four years and do the master's. I'd keep investing £400 a month. Then I'd move into policy or a charity that helps poorer schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that ten years that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That governments will waste the decade. Ten years can disappear in committees. And I'd still worry for people like my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your students in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real skills. Being able to question a machine, work in a team, fix things with their hands. I'd want the kids at my school to come out ahead for once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for me so much, but for people like my dad and Maureen in our office, who'd have no time at all. What would help is public money for retraining and AI tools that schools own, so poorer kids aren't left behind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether teachers get a say. Every time new tech arrives in schools, it's bought by someone who's never taught. I'd want teachers in the room from day one.
